body:
Why was labour legislation introduced?

As modern factories expanded, the conditions of industrial employment became a public issue. Long hours and the employment of young children were important concerns. Colonial legislation gradually regulated certain aspects of factory work, although its coverage was limited and enforcement was not always effective.

It is important to distinguish factory legislation, which regulated conditions within covered workplaces, from trade-union legislation, which dealt with workers' collective organisations.

The Factories Acts of 1881, 1891 and 1911

The first Indian Factories Act was enacted in 1881. It mainly introduced limited protection for children in certain larger factories. Among its provisions were a minimum employment age of 7 years and a maximum of 9 working hours per day for covered child workers.

The Factories Act of 1891 expanded regulation. It raised the minimum employment age for children to 9 years and reduced their permitted working hours to 7 per day. It also introduced further provisions relating to women, rest and holidays.

Further changes followed under the Factories Act of 1911, including additional regulation of working conditions and hours.

These rules did not immediately establish a modern universal system of labour protection. They applied to specified categories of factories and workers. Many employees in small workshops, agriculture and plantations remained outside important parts of factory regulation.

Early associations of workers

Workers began forming associations to present demands collectively rather than individually. Narayan Meghaji Lokhande is associated with the Bombay Mill Hands Association, founded in 1890. The association raised concerns relating to the conditions of mill workers.

The Madras Labour Union, established in 1918, is associated with B. P. Wadia. It was one of the earliest modern organised trade unions in India.

The earlier Bombay association and the Madras Labour Union should not be confused merely because both are described in accounts of India's early labour movement.

All India Trade Union Congress, 1920

As industrial employment and strikes increased, labour leaders sought coordination beyond individual factories and cities.

The All India Trade Union Congress, commonly abbreviated AITUC, was founded in Bombay in 1920. Its first president was Lala Lajpat Rai. N. M. Joshi was another important figure in the early organisation of trade unions.

AITUC provided a national platform for labour demands. Its creation also demonstrated the increasing interaction between working-class politics and wider debates about political rights and colonial rule.

The Trade Unions Act, 1926

The Trade Unions Act, 1926 established a legal framework for the registration of trade unions and provided specified protections for registered unions and their activities in relation to trade disputes. These included immunity from certain civil suits over trade-dispute activities and protection for office-bearers and members against criminal-conspiracy liability for agreements furthering permitted union objects, unless the agreement was to commit an offence.

Registration did not mean that every industrial action became lawful or that a union's demands had to be accepted. The Act concerned the legal position of collective organisations; it was not the same kind of legislation as the Factories Acts regulating work within factories.

Prelims focus

  • 1881: First Indian Factories Act; limited protection for child workers.
  • 1891: Factories Act expanded regulation and raised the minimum employment age for children to 9.
  • 1890: Bombay Mill Hands Association; N. M. Lokhande.
  • 1918: Madras Labour Union; B. P. Wadia.
  • 1920: AITUC founded in Bombay; first president Lala Lajpat Rai.
  • Trap: The Trade Unions Act of 1926 dealt with union registration and legal protections, not the same subject as the Factories Act of 1881.

[Sources: V. V. Giri National Labour Institute, Performance of Labour Administration, ch. II, Statutory Provisions and Child Labour in India: An Overview; National Commission on Labour, Report of the Second National Commission on Labour, Vol. I, section on the historical development of labour legislation, p. 104; Government of NCT of Delhi, Labour Department, The Trade Unions Act, 1926, historical introduction; Government of India, The Trade Unions Act, 1926, provisions on registration and legal protections; online sources consulted 20 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Parallel timelines distinguish the Factories Acts from workers’ organisations and the Trade Unions Act, from 1881 to 1926.
pictures.caption: Factory legislation and organised labour: parallel developments.

title: Colonial Factory Laws and the Growth of Trade Unions

body:
Why did workers organise strikes?

A strike is a collective stoppage of work used by workers to press demands or express opposition. In colonial India, strikes could arise from wages, working hours, dismissals and treatment by employers. Some also became connected with nationalist politics.

Industrial workers did not always have the same interests or political methods. Different organisations could favour negotiation, non-violent protest or more confrontational action. The important connection is that factory workers increasingly acted together rather than relying only on individual appeals to employers.

The Ahmedabad Mill Strike of 1918

The Ahmedabad Mill Strike of 1918 was an important labour dispute in Gujarat's cotton textile industry. Its immediate background included disagreement over wages and the withdrawal or reduction of an allowance associated with the plague period.

Mahatma Gandhi intervened in support of the workers and encouraged disciplined non-violent action. Anasuya Sarabhai played an important role in organising Ahmedabad textile workers.

Gandhi undertook a fast during the dispute, and the conflict moved towards settlement through arbitration. The episode is remembered as an important early example of Gandhian methods being applied to an industrial labour dispute.

The immediate grievance was about workers' wages. It was not a demand by cultivators to suspend land revenue.

Majoor Mahajan Sangh, 1920

The Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association, also known as Majoor Mahajan Sangh, was established in 1920. Anasuya Sarabhai was central to its development, with Gandhi closely associated with the approach to labour relations.

The organisation represented textile workers and became an important institution in Gujarat's labour history. Its emphasis on organisation, negotiation and industrial relations differed from the immediate purpose of a temporary strike.

Ahmedabad therefore has a distinct place in the history of both early trade unionism and the application of Gandhian methods to workers' grievances.

Other links between workers and nationalist politics

Labour participation in political protest was not limited to Ahmedabad.

  • Bombay, 1908: Textile workers participated in strikes and protests following the conviction and imprisonment of nationalist leader Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
  • Assam, 1921: During the Non-Cooperation period, many tea plantation workers attempted to leave the estates. For them, freedom included the ability to return to their villages.
  • Bombay, 1928: A major textile strike illustrated the growth of organised working-class action, including more radical labour politics.

These examples show several different relationships with nationalism. Ahmedabad's dispute centred on wages and Gandhian mediation. The Bombay protests of 1908 connected industrial workers directly with a nationalist political event. Assam plantation workers interpreted the promise of freedom in terms of their own restrictions on movement.

Distinguishing major Gujarat movements

Three important Gandhian-era movements can be separated by their participants and immediate demands:

  • Ahmedabad, 1918: Textile mill workers sought a settlement of their wage dispute.
  • Kheda, 1918: Cultivators demanded relief from land revenue following crop failure.
  • Bardoli, 1928: Cultivators resisted an increase in the government's land-revenue assessment under Vallabhbhai Patel's leadership.

The fact that Ahmedabad and Kheda occurred in the same year does not make them the same movement.

One connected history of colonial resistance

Tribal, peasant and labour movements shared an objection to forms of power that threatened livelihoods and rights. Their immediate demands nevertheless remained specific: customary land and forest access for many tribal communities; rent, revenue, credit and cultivation rights for peasants; and wages, working conditions and collective representation for industrial workers.

During the nationalist period, these struggles increasingly interacted with larger political movements. This interaction did not erase their distinct local causes. A correct account of any movement must therefore identify its people, place, period, immediate grievance and principal leadership.

Prelims focus

  • Ahmedabad Mill Strike: 1918, textile workers, wage dispute.
  • Gandhi and Anasuya Sarabhai are associated with the Ahmedabad labour movement.
  • Ahmedabad Textile Labour Association, or Majoor Mahajan Sangh: 1920.
  • Bombay textile-worker protests of 1908 were connected with the imprisonment of Bal Gangadhar Tilak.
  • Kheda, 1918, concerned agricultural revenue; Bardoli, 1928, opposed an enhanced land-revenue assessment.
  • Trap: Ahmedabad Mill Strike and Kheda Satyagraha both occurred in 1918, but the former was a labour dispute and the latter a peasant revenue movement.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History–Part III, Class 12, ch. Mahatma Gandhi and the Nationalist Movement, section The Making and Unmaking of Non-Cooperation; NCERT, Our Pasts–III, Class 8, 2020–21, ch. The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World–II, Class 10, ch. 2, Nationalism in India, section Swaraj in the Plantations; Ahmedabad Municipal Corporation, Heritage City, Majoor Mahajan Sangh; Cambridge University Press, account of Bombay textile-worker protests following Tilak's conviction in 1908; online sources consulted 20 November 2026.]

title: Ahmedabad Mill Workers, Strikes and the Links Between Labour and Nationalism
